correctness.rationale: The precise real L^p(mu) assertion requires two disjoint measurable finite positive-measure sets and 0<=lambda<=1, including p=1 and p=infinity. Write m=1-lambda. For 1<p<=2, apply Clarkson to lambda x and m y: the sum of q-th powers of their plus/minus norms is <=2(lambda^p+m^p)^(q/p), q=p/(p-1); thus their minimum is <=(lambda^p+m^p)^(1/p). For 2<=p<infinity, Hanner gives the sum of p-th powers <=(lambda+m)^p+|lambda-m|^p=1+|2lambda-1|^p; dividing by two bounds the minimum. At p=1 and infinity the triangle inequality bounds by 1. Normalize disjoint indicators e,f. For 1<=p<=2, x=e,y=f are unit, satisfy ||e+t f||_p>=(||e||=1) for every t, and have both chord norms (lambda^p+m^p)^(1/p). For 2<=p<infinity, x=2^(-1/p)(e+f),y=2^(-1/p)(e-f) are unit and their Lp smooth norming-integral cancels exactly, so x is Birkhoff-James orthogonal to y. The plus/minus p-th powers equal [1+|2lambda-1|^p]/2. For infinity x=e+f,y=e-f are norm-one, ||x+t y||_infinity=max(|1+t|,|1-t|)>=1 and both weighted norms =1. Endpoints lambda=0,1 are included and p=2 branches agree. This is a universal inequality plus explicit sharp pairs, not a finite experiment.
residual_risks: No classification of all norming pairs. Two-disjoint-finite-positive-measure-piece hypothesis is essential; one-dimensional Lp is excluded. No statement for complex Lp or generic Banach lattices.
